L9: # Title:DeepSec: Deciding Equivalence Properties for Security Protocols -- Improved theory and practice
L10: 
L11: Authors:【6†Vincent Cheval】, 【7†Steve Kremer】, 【8†Itsaka Rakotonirina】
L12: 
L13: View a PDF of the paper titled DeepSec: Deciding Equivalence Properties for Security Protocols -- Improved theory and practice, by Vincent Cheval and 2 other authors
L14: 
L15: 【9†View PDF】
L16: > Abstract:Automated verification has become an essential part in the security evaluation of cryptographic protocols. In this context privacy-type properties are often modelled by indistinguishability statements, expressed as behavioural equivalences in a process calculus. In this paper we contribute both to the theory and practice of this verification problem.
L17: We establish new complexity results for static equivalence, trace equivalence and labelled bisimilarity and provide a decision procedure for these equivalences in the case of a bounded number of protocol sessions. Our procedure is the first to decide trace equivalence and labelled bisimilarity exactly for a large variety of cryptographic primitives -- those that can be represented by a subterm convergent destructor rewrite system. We also implemented the procedure in a new tool, DeepSec.
L18: We showed through extensive experiments that it is significantly more efficient than other similar tools, while at the same time raises the scope of the protocols that can be analysed.

L0@P0: DEEPSEC: Deciding Equivalence Properties in Security Protocols
L1@P0: Theory and Practice
L2@P0: Vincent Cheval, Steve Kremer, Itsaka Rakotonirina
L3@P0: Inria & LORIA
L4@P0: Abstract—Automated verification has become an essential part
L5@P0: in the security evaluation of cryptographic protocols. Recently,
L6@P0: there has been a considerable effort to lift the theory and
L7@P0: tool support that existed for reachability properties to the
L8@P0: more complex case of equivalence properties. In this paper
L9@P0: we contribute both to the theory and practice of this verification problem. We establish new complexity results for
L10@P0: static equivalence, trace equivalence and labelled bisimilarity
L11@P0: and provide a decision procedure for these equivalences in
L12@P0: the case of a bounded number of sessions. Our procedure is
L13@P0: the first to decide trace equivalence and labelled bisimilarity
L14@P0: exactly for a large variety of cryptographic primitives—those
L15@P0: that can be represented by a subterm convergent destructor
L16@P0: rewrite system. We implemented the procedure in a new tool,
L17@P0: DEEPSEC. We showed through extensive experiments that it
L18@P0: is significantly more efficient than other similar tools, while at
L19@P0: the same time raises the scope of the protocols that can be
L20@P0: analysed.
L21@P0: 1. Introduction
L22@P0: The use of automated, formal methods has become
L23@P0: indispensable for analysing complex security protocols, such
L24@P0: as those for authentication, key exchange and secure channel
L25@P0: establishment. Nowadays there exist mature, fully automated
L26@P0: such analysers; among others AVISPA [11], ProVerif [17],
L27@P0: Scyther [33], Tamarin [45] or Maude-NPA [44]. These tools
L28@P0: operate in so-called symbolic models, rooted in the seminal
L29@P0: work by Dolev and Yao [35]: the attacker has full control
L30@P0: of the communication network, unbounded computational
L31@P0: power, but cryptography is idealised. This model is well
L32@P0: suited for finding attacks in the protocol logic, and tools have
L33@P0: indeed been extremely effective in discovering this kind of
L34@P0: flaw or proving their absence.
L35@P0: While most works investigate reachability properties, a
L36@P0: recent trend consists in adapting the tools—and the underlying theory—for the more complex indistinguishability
L37@P0: properties. Such properties are generally modelled as a
L38@P0: behavioural equivalence (bisimulation or trace equivalence)
L39@P0: in a dedicated process calculus such as the Spi [6] or applied
L40@P0: pi calculus [5]. A typical example is real-or-random secrecy:
L41@P0: after interacting with a protocol, an adversary is unable
L42@P0: to distinguish the real secret used in the protocol from a
L43@P0: random value. Privacy-type properties can also be expressed
L44@P0: as such: anonymity may be modeled as the adversary’s
L45@P0: inability to distinguish two instances of a protocol executed
L46@P0: by different agents; vote privacy [34] has been expressed as
L47@P0: indistinguishability of the situations where the votes of two
L48@P0: agents have been swapped or not; unlinkability [8] is seen
L49@P0: as indistinguishability of two sessions, either both executed
L50@P0: by the same agent A, or by two different agents A and B.
L51@P0: Related work. The problem of analysing security protocols
L52@P0: is undecidable in general but several decidable subclasses
L53@P0: have been identified. While many complexity results are
L54@P0: known for trace properties [36], [42], the case of behavioural
L55@P0: equivalences remains mostly open. When the attacker is
L56@P0: an eavesdropper and cannot interact with the protocol, the
L57@P0: indistinguishability problem—static equivalence—has been
L58@P0: shown PTIME for large classes of cryptographic primitives [3], [27], [29]. For active attackers, bounding the
L59@P0: number of protocol sessions is often sufficient to obtain
L60@P0: decidability [42] and is of practical interest: most real-life
L61@P0: attacks indeed only require a small number of sessions.
L62@P0: In this context Baudet [14], and later Chevalier and Rusinowtich [24], showed that real-or-random secrecy was coNP
L63@P0: for cryptographic primitives that can be modelled as subterm convergent rewrite systems, by checking whether two
L64@P0: constraint systems admit the same set of solutions. These
L65@P0: procedures do however not allow for else branches, nor
L66@P0: do they verify trace equivalence in full generality. In [23],
L67@P0: Cheval et al. have used Baudet’s procedure as a black box to
L68@P0: verify trace equivalence of determinate processes. This class
L69@P0: of processes is however insufficient for most anonymity
L70@P0: properties. Finally, decidability results for an unbounded
L71@P0: number of sessions were proposed in [26], [25], but with
L72@P0: severe restrictions on processes and equational theories.
L73@P0: Tool support also exists for verifying equivalence properties. We start discussing tools that are limited to a bounded
L74@P0: number of sessions. The SPEC tool [46], [47] verifies a
L75@P0: sound symbolic bisimulation, but is restricted to particular
L76@P0: cryptographic primitives (pairing, encryption, signatures and
L77@P0: hash functions) and does not allow for else branches. The
L78@P0: APTE tool [20] covers the same primitives but allows else
L79@P0: branches and decides trace equivalence exactly. On the
L80@P0: contrary, the AKISS tool [19] allows for user-defined cryptographic primitives. Partial correctness of AKISS is shown
L81@P0: for primitives modelled by an arbitrary convergent rewrite
L82@P0: system that has the finite variant property [28]. Termination
L83@P0-1: is additionally shown for subterm convergent rewrite systems. However, AKISS does only decide trace equivalencefor a class of determinate processes; for other processes
L84@P1: trace equivalence can be both over- and under-approximated
L85@P1: which proved to be sufficient on many examples. The recent
L86@P1: SAT-EQUIV tool [30] uses a different approach: it relies on
L87@P1: Graph Planning and SAT solving to verify trace equivalence,
L88@P1: rather than a dedicated procedure. The tool is extremely
L89@P1: efficient and several orders of magnitude faster than other
L90@P1: tools. It does however not guarantee termination and is
L91@P1: currently restricted to pairing and symmetric encryption
L92@P1: and only considers a class of simple processes (a subclass
L93@P1: of determinate processes) that satisfy a type-compliance
L94@P1: condition. These restrictions severely limit its scope.
L95@P1: Other tools support verification of equivalence properties, even for an unbounded number of sessions. This
L96@P1: is the case of ProVerif [15], Tamarin [13] and Maude
L97@P1: NPA [44] which all allow for user-defined cryptographic
L98@P1: primitives. However, given that the underlying problem is

L308: As a consequence, a universal co-Büchi automaton for ${𝖶}_{𝒜,R}$ can be derived from one for ${\text{W}}^{\prime }$. Let us explain how we build it. First, ${L}_{\text{join}}$ is recognizable by a deterministic (safety) automaton with two states. Then, the complement of ${\text{W}}^{\prime }$ roughly corresponds to the intersection of ${L}_{\text{join}}$ with ${\mathrm{𝖲𝖠𝖳}}_{k,V\cup R}$ and with the complement of $L({𝒜}_{stx})$.
L309: The non-deterministic parity automaton for ${\mathrm{𝖲𝖠𝖳}}_{k,V\cup R}$ can be translated into a non-deterministic Büchi one in polynomial time. In addition, as $𝒜$ is a universal co-Büchi CA, the complement of $L({𝒜}_{stx})$ is also recognized by a non-deterministic Büchi automaton. Last, the intersection of two non-deterministic Büchi automata is known to be a non-deterministic Büchi automaton of polynomial size which can built in PTime (see for instance [【41†1】]). $◀$
L310: #### Proof sketch of Theorem 【19†10】.
L311: 
L312: The Transfer Lemma (Lemma 【38†13】) reduces the register-bounded synthesis problem to a synthesis problem over a finite alphabet, whose specification is $\omega $-regular by Lemma 【42†14】. This problem is decidable by Büchi-Landweber’s Theorem. $◀$
L313: #### Data domains with the completion property.
L314: 
L315: Theorem 【19†10】 is established for data domains with effective $\omega $-regular satisfiability. We prove that any data domain satisfying the completion property has $\omega $-regular satisfiability. Intuitively, we build a safety automaton that stores the last constraint read and checks that two consecutive constraints are compatible.
L316: ###### Lemma 15.
L317: 
L318: Let $𝒟$ be a decidable completable data domain, then $𝒟$ has $\omega $-regular satisfiability. Moreover, if $𝒟$ is decidable in ExpTime, then a deterministic parity automaton recognizing ${\mathrm{𝖲𝖠𝖳}}_{k,X}$ can be constructed that has $exp(k.|X|)$ states and 2 priorities.
L319: ###### $\textcolor[rgb]{0.309803921568627,0.309803921568627,0.329411764705882}{▶}$ Remark 16.
L320: 
L321: In the statement, we require that the existential first-order theory of $𝒟$ is decidable. In fact we only need decidability of the satisfiability of conjunctions of constraints and not any formula, this problem is generally easier.
L322: 
L323: We can now state the main result of this section:
L324: ###### Theorem 17.
L325: 
L326: Let $𝒟$ be a decidable completable data domain (resp. decidable in ExpTime). Then register-bounded synthesis from $\mathrm{𝖢𝖫𝖳𝖫}(𝒟)$ is decidable (resp. 2ExpTime-c). It is 2ExpTime-hard for any fixed number of registers $r\ge 2$.
L327: #### Proof sketch.
L328: 
L329: To prove the upper bound, we first build from a $\mathrm{𝖢𝖫𝖳𝖫}$ formula $\mathrm{\Phi }$ an equivalent CA $𝒜$, using Proposition 【43†5】. Then, using Lemmas 【38†13】, 【42†14】, 【44†15】, realizability of $\mathrm{\Phi }$ reduces to that of ${𝖶}_{𝒜,R}$, which can be recognized by a universal co-Büchi automaton whose size is exponential in $|\mathrm{\Phi }|$, $k$ and $|R|$. Last, realizability for specifications expressed by universal co-Büchi automata can be decided in ExpTime [【31†20】].
L330: For the lower bound, we reduce the problem of LTL synthesis (over finite alphabets), which is already 2ExpTime-c [【36†21】], to bounded register synthesis with two registers, over domain $𝒟$. Intuitively, we use two distinct data values in order to encode the two boolean values, and add constraints in the formula in order to ensure that the register transducer uses two registers to store these data values all along the execution. $◀$
L331: ###### $\textcolor[rgb]{0.309803921568627,0.309803921568627,0.329411764705882}{▶}$ Remark 18.
L332: 
L333: In Theorem 【45†17】, the lower bound already holds for two registers, and also if $𝒟$ has an existential first-order theory decidable in PTime. Moreover, this lower bound holds for any data domain, as long as equality is definable.
L334: We have seen in Lemma 【46†1】 that $(𝔻,=,{d}_{0})$ and $(\mathbb{Q},<,0)$ are completable data domains. In addition, it is easily seen that the existential first-order theory of $(𝔻,=,{d}_{0})$ is decidable in NP, as well as for $(\mathbb{Q},<,0)$. As a consequence of Theorem 【45†17】, we obtain:
L335: ###### Corollary 19.
L336: 
L337: Register-bounded synthesis from $\mathrm{𝖢𝖫𝖳𝖫}$ $(𝔻,=,{d}_{0})$ and $\mathrm{𝖢𝖫𝖳𝖫}$ $(\mathbb{Q},<,0)$ is 2ExpTime-complete.
L338: ## 5 $𝝎$-Regularly approximable data domains
L339: Another important setting is the data domain $(\mathbb{N},<,0)$. As said before, it is not completable, but worse than that, its set of satisfiable constraint words ${\mathrm{𝖲𝖠𝖳}}_{k,X}$ is not regular (see e.g. [【47†22】, 【15†9】]). Actually, when considering only finite words, this set is regular, but it turns out that it is not regular when considering infinite words. Here is an example to illustrate this discrepancy.
L340: We define $\text{decrease}=({x}^{(1)}<{x}^{(0)}\wedge {y}^{(1)}={y}^{(0)})$ and $\text{reset}=({x}^{(1)}={y}^{(0)}\wedge {y}^{(1)}={y}^{(0)})$. Then we look at the family of constraint words $\text{reset}.{\text{decrease}}^{{i}_{1}}.\text{reset}.{\text{decrease}}^{{i}_{2}}.\text{reset}.{\text{decrease}}^{{i}_{3}}\mathrm{\dots }$.
L341: Depending on the sequence ${({i}_{n})}_{n\ge 0}$, the constraint word will or will not be satisfiable: if ${({i}_{n})}_{n\ge 0}$ has an upper bound then by picking the first value for $y$ big enough we can build a satisfying valuation, but otherwise the constraint word is not satisfiable. In this section, we will show an extension of the previous framework that allows to capture such data domains.
L342: ### 5.1 General approach
L343: 
L344: Let $X$ be a set of variables and $k\in \mathbb{N}$. We let $\mathrm{𝖫𝖠𝖲𝖲𝖮}\subseteq {(ℳ{𝒞}_{X}^{(k)})}^{\omega }$ denote the set of ultimately periodic constraint words (or lasso-shaped word), formally $\mathrm{𝖫𝖠𝖲𝖲𝖮}=\{u.{v}^{\omega }\mid u,v\in 𝒞_{X}^{(k)}{}_{}{}^{\ast }\}$.
L345: ###### Definition 20.
L346: 
L347: We say that $𝒟$ is effectively $\omega $-regularly approximable if there exists a computable function which associates with every $k,X$, an automaton recognizing an $\omega $-regular language denoted ${\mathrm{𝖰𝖲𝖠𝖳}}_{k,X}\subseteq {(ℳ{𝒞}_{X}^{(k)})}^{\omega }$ such that ${\mathrm{𝖲𝖠𝖳}}_{k,X}\subseteq {\mathrm{𝖰𝖲𝖠𝖳}}_{k,X}$ and ${\mathrm{𝖲𝖠𝖳}}_{k,X}\cap \mathrm{𝖫𝖠𝖲𝖲𝖮}={\mathrm{𝖰𝖲𝖠𝖳}}_{k,X}\cap \mathrm{𝖫𝖠𝖲𝖲𝖮}$.
L348: ###### $\textcolor[rgb]{0.309803921568627,0.309803921568627,0.329411764705882}{▶}$ Remark 21.
L349: 
L350: ${\mathrm{𝖰𝖲𝖠𝖳}}_{k,X}$ can be thought of as an over-approximation of ${\mathrm{𝖲𝖠𝖳}}_{k,X}$ which is exact on lasso-shaped words.
L351: ###### Theorem 22.
L352: 
L353: Let $𝒟$ be an effectively $\omega $-regularly approximable data domain. Then register-bounded synthesis from specifications expressed as universal co-Büchi CA is decidable.

L355: Let $𝒜$ be a universal co-Büchi CA over $𝒟$, an $\omega $-regularly approximable data domain, and $R$ be a set of registers. Fix ${\mathrm{𝖰𝖲𝖠𝖳}}_{k,V\cup R}\subseteq {(ℳ{𝒞}_{V\cup R}^{(k)})}^{\omega }$ as given in Definition 【48†20】. We define the following language by:
